title: The Effects of Working Memory Load on Auditory Distraction in Adults With Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder
research_question: To investigate whether adults with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (aADHD), compared to healthy controls, demonstrate heightened cortical responses to task-irrelevant acoustic stimulation whilst engaged in a visual working memory (WM) task, and to explore whether cortical attenuation of task-irrelevant acoustic stimulation is associated with individual differences in WM capacity. Additionally, to test for between-group differences in auditory-Salience Network (SN) connectivity during an Auditory Target Detection (ATD) task.

participants.description: 17 aADHD (11 females, 6 males; M=28 years, SD=7.0) and 17 typically developed controls (13 females, 4 males; M=25.5 years, SD=5.5). All participants had normal hearing thresholds (<20 dB HL). ADHD group had significantly higher ASRS scores (inattentive, hyperactivity/impulsivity, total). 15/17 ADHD participants were on stimulant medication (abstained for 48h prior to testing), 2 unmedicated. 5 ADHD participants had SSRI medication, 1 had lamotrigine.
participants.recruitment: Not explicitly stated beyond 'We recruited two groups of participants: clinically stable adults with ADHD and healthy controls.'

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Visual n-back task: Sequence of 15 letters (K, M, Q, R, S, T, W) presented for 500ms, followed by 1022ms fixation cross. White text on black background, font size 18 points. 0-back, 1-back, and 2-back conditions.

Auditory stimuli (n-back task): Monotonous tonal signal with occasional deviant pitch (1000 Hz) amidst standard tones (500 Hz). Tones 150ms (rise/fall 22ms), presented every 104ms. Perceived loudness -16 LUFS, ~75 dB SPL. Participants instructed to ignore.

Auditory Target Detection (ATD) task: Participants detected deviant tones (1000 Hz) amidst standard tones (500 Hz) in noise. Tones 150ms (rise/fall 22ms), presented every 104ms. Perceived loudness -16 LUFS, ~75 dB SPL. Participants instructed to attend.
Background noise: Echo planar imaging (EPI) gradient noise, attenuated to ~58 dB SPL by active noise canceling headphones.

measures.construct: Task Performance (Response Times, Accuracy, False Alarms) for n-back task
Task Performance (Response Times, Accuracy, False Alarms) for ATD task

mechanisms: Cognitive control regulates the locus of attention and ignores environmental distractions.
Working memory (WM) capacity shields against auditory distraction by maintaining steadfast attention and deploying inhibitory mechanisms that suppress neural responses to task-irrelevant sounds.
Challenging cognitive requirements increase attentional engagement and decrease susceptibility for distraction.
The Salience Network (SN) is involved in vigilant anticipation, detection, and response-mediation of behaviorally salient stimuli.

Increased functional communications between auditory and SN in aADHD during the ATD task may be an adaptive mechanism to facilitate successful oddball detection and reduce erroneous responding under suboptimal listening conditions.
Heightened cortical responses to task-irrelevant auditory stimulation can negatively impact task performance and contribute to subjective experiences of auditory distraction.
aADHD individuals may need to deploy more cognitive effort to inhibit distraction, potentially contributing to higher perceived stress and related pathologies.
implementation_implications: Clinical interventions should address adapting work/study environments to minimize disturbance for individuals with aADHD.
Psychoeducation can help improve stress and time-management for aADHD.
Early interventions are needed to help aADHD adapt study/work environments, develop effective coping strategies, and minimize risk for chronic stress and anxiety.

tables.description: Group descriptives for education, hearing acuity and neuropsychological assessments of ADHD-related symptomology.
Descriptives and one-way ANOVA results for group comparisons of working memory (WM) capacity and in-scanner task performance on the n-back and auditory target detection (ATD) conditions.

limitations: Comparisons of ROIs and networks are difficult across literature due to differences in nomenclature and methods of definition.
Scanner noise was audible throughout the experiment, potentially interfering with performance on the ATD task and leading to impulsive false-alarm responding.
Small sample size and relatively high-functioning ADHD sample limit generalizability and may underestimate overall group differences.
Gender imbalance in the ADHD sample (more females than males).
Comorbidities (around half of the ADHD sample were on stable SSRI medication).
WM capacity measures used might not have been sufficiently sensitive indexes for the type of control mechanisms involved in the 2-back condition.

paper_metadata.title: The Effects of Working Memory Load on Auditory Distraction in Adults With Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder
paper_metadata.crossref_title: The Effects of Working Memory Load on Auditory Distraction in Adults With Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Cognitive control provides us with the ability tointer alia, regulate the locus of attention and ignore environmental distractions in accordance with our goals. Auditory distraction is a frequently cited symptom in adults with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (aADHD)–yet few task-based fMRI studies have explored whether deficits in cognitive control (associated with the disorder) impedes on the ability to suppress/compensate for exogenously evoked cortical responses to noise in this population. In the current study, we explored the effects of auditory distraction as function of working memory (WM) load. Participants completed two tasks: an auditory target detection (ATD) task in which the goal was to actively detect salient oddball tones amidst a stream of standard tones in noise, and a visualn-back task consisting of 0-, 1-, and 2-back WM conditions whilst concurrently ignoring the same tonal signal from the ATD task. Results indicated that our sample of young aADHD (n= 17), compared to typically developed controls (n= 17), had difficulty attenuating auditory cortical responses to the task-irrelevant sound when WM demands were high (2-back). Heightened auditory activity to task-irrelevant sound was associated with both poorer WM performance and symptomatic inattentiveness. In the ATD task, we observed a significant increase in functional communications between auditory and salience networks in aADHD. Because performance outcomes were on par with controls for this task, we suggest that this increased functional connectivity in aADHD was likely an adaptive mechanism for suboptimal listening conditions. Taken together, our results indicate that aADHD are more susceptible to noise interference when they are engaged in a primary task. The ability to cope with auditory distraction appears to be related to the WM demands of the task and thus the capacity to deploy cognitive control.

environmental_features: Auditory stimuli (irrelevant speech, white noise, silence) presented via headphones
Visual stimuli (letters or numbers) for working memory task presented on a monitor
stimulus_description.duration_exposure: Multiple blocks of 5-10 minutes each, totaling approximately 30-60 minutes of task exposure

instruments_used.name: N-back Task
instruments_used.description: A continuous performance task requiring participants to respond if the current stimulus matches the stimulus 'n' steps back.

instruments_used.name: Auditory Distraction Stimuli
instruments_used.description: Pre-recorded irrelevant speech (e.g., single-speaker narrative) and white noise presented binaurally.

instruments_used.name: Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS)
instruments_used.description: A self-report questionnaire based on DSM-IV or DSM-5 criteria for adult ADHD.

instruments_used.name: Reaction Time (RT)
instruments_used.description: Time taken to respond to target stimuli in the N-back task.

instruments_used.name: Accuracy
instruments_used.description: Percentage of correct responses in the N-back task.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Working memory is a limited-capacity system responsible for temporary storage and manipulation of information, susceptible to interference.
Increased cognitive load consumes limited processing resources, making individuals more vulnerable to distraction.

theory_commitments.theory_name: Models of ADHD (e.g., Executive Dysfunction Models)
theory_commitments.specific_claim: Individuals with ADHD exhibit deficits in executive functions, leading to impaired working memory and increased susceptibility to distraction, especially under high cognitive load.

mechanism_chain.description: Increased working memory load consumes limited cognitive resources, reducing the capacity to filter out irrelevant auditory stimuli. This resource depletion is hypothesized to be more pronounced in individuals with ADHD, leading to greater distraction and impaired task performance.
